newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippines to spend $2 bln on defence forces.
newsitem.headline: Philippines to spend $2 bln on defence forces.

text.p: The Philippines will spend about $2 billion over the next five years to modernise its defence forces with more fighter planes and patrol ships, Defence Secretary Renato De Villa said.
"We are looking at spending 50 billion pesos ($2 billion) over the next five years," De Villa told Reuters in an interview on Thursday.
The five-year weapons acquisition plan is the first phase of a 15-year programme during which the country would spend up to a total of $12 billion, he said.
"We are initially looking at buying 36 planes but in the first phase we will go for 18," De Villa said. "For the Navy, we want a small fleet consisting of patrol craft and offshore patrol vessels."
Manila's plans to upgrade its defence forces have brought arms makers and dealers swarming into the country.
At a defence exhibition held in Manila two weeks ago, Israeli armaments manufacturers vied with American, British and French firms to explain the advantages of their weaponry.

Local media reports said the Philippine air force had short-listed four types of fighter aircraft but De Villa declined to confirm the reports, saying: "I am not going to be drawn into naming brands ...for obvious reasons."
"We are looking for the right multi-role aircraft that will constitute the main component of our air defence system," he said.
The reports said the air force had narrowed its choice to F-16 or F-18 fighter jets from the United States, the Mirage from France, the MiG 29 from Russia and an Israeli aircraft.
The Philippines is also negotiating with the British government to buy Hong Kong-based frigates that will become surplus when the territory returns to China on July 1.
"But the budget for this is separate from the modernisation programme," De Villa said.
Asked if the Philippines perceived any military threats in the region, De Villa said: "That is farthest from our minds.

"It is a modest modernisation and we are not doing this in terms of addressing a specific threat in the region ... but it is our duty to ensure that we are prepared for any eventuality just like other countries around us."

Tensions rose between the Philippines and China in 1995 after China built what Manila called military structures in the disputed Spratly Islands in the South China Sea. Beijing said the structures were shelters for fishermen.

Since then, the two countries have steered clear of the territorial row over the Spratlys. The cluster of potentially oil-rich isles, reefs and shoals are claimed wholly or in part by China, the Philippines, Taiwan, Vietnam, Malaysia and Brunei.
The Philippine armed forces has been one of the most poorly equipped in the region and its ageing boats and planes have created both disastrous as well as embarassing situations.

When the Philippines took a team of foreign journalists on a warship to the disputed Spratlys in an effort to prove that the Chinese had built military structures, the ship broke down and had to be towed to the nearest port.
Its war planes have also routinely failed.
In January, a Philippine air force fighter jet crashed during a fly-past ceremony, killing the pilot and a man on the ground. This was the seventh air force plane to crash since 1991.
